note: Original passages written for this app (docs/03 §4 route 2), flagged origin 'llm'. Grade-5 band: FK 4.5–6.5, 11–17 words per sentence, 250–500 words — verified by scripts/check-passages.js. Each carries a 5–6 question set: literal/evidence (RL.5.1), theme (RL.5.2), vocabulary in context (L.5.4a), craft/structure/POV (RL.5.4–6), and one short-text 'quote the sentence' item.

passages.title: The Two Goats on the Bridge
passages.text: High in the mountains, where the river ran fast and cold, a narrow bridge crossed a deep gorge. The bridge was nothing more than a single wooden plank, worn smooth by many years of hooves. It was so narrow that only one animal could cross at a time, and everyone in the valley knew it. One bright morning, a white goat stepped onto the plank from the eastern bank. At exactly the same moment, a black goat started across from the western side. They met in the middle, with the water roaring far below their feet. "Step back," said the white goat, "because I was already on the bridge before you." The black goat tossed her head and refused to move a single inch. "You step back," she answered, "because I am in a hurry and my side is closer." Neither goat would give way, and the argument grew louder with every word. The white goat lowered his horns, and the black goat lowered hers in reply. They pushed and shoved until the old plank began to tremble beneath them. A moment later, both goats tumbled together into the freezing river. They scrambled to the bank, dripping and ashamed, while the birds laughed from the trees. That evening, two sheep arrived at the same bridge from opposite directions. The first sheep saw the other coming and understood the problem immediately. Without saying a word, she lay down flat on the plank and waited patiently. The second sheep stepped carefully over her woolly back and continued on her way. Then the first sheep rose, shook herself, and crossed to the other side. The goats watched all of this from the bank, still shivering in the evening wind. "We could easily have done that," said the white goat in a quiet voice. The black goat shook the last drops of water from her ears. "Yes," she agreed, "but we were far too busy being right." From that day on, whenever the two goats met on a narrow path, one of them always stepped aside first.

questions.stem: Why could only one animal cross the bridge at a time?
options: The bridge was a single narrow plank.
The goats were afraid of the sheep.

distractor_rationale.B: the noise is mentioned but is not the reason

questions.explanation: The text says the bridge was a single wooden plank, so narrow that only one animal could cross.
questions.rule: RL.5.1 — find the detail the text states directly.

questions.stem: What is the theme of this fable?
options: Being right matters more than being safe.
Giving way a little can save everyone a great deal of trouble.
Never cross a bridge in the morning.
questions.explanation: The sheep solve the problem by yielding; the goats learn to step aside.
questions.rule: RL.5.2 — theme from how characters respond to a challenge.

questions.stem: "They scrambled to the bank, dripping and ashamed." What does "ashamed" mean here?
options: embarrassed about what they had done

distractor_rationale.C: wet, not the same as ashamed
distractor_rationale.D: the goats blame themselves, not the river

questions.explanation: They feel bad because their stubbornness made them fall.
questions.rule: L.5.4a — use the sentence around the word.

questions.stem: How are the sheep different from the goats?
options: The sheep solve the problem when one lies down so the other can pass.
The sheep swim across the river.
questions.explanation: The sheep cooperate instead of pushing.

questions.stem: The story is told by a narrator who is not a character. How does this affect what we learn?
options: We only hear the white goat's private thoughts.
We see what both goats and the sheep do, from the outside.
We never find out what the sheep did.

distractor_rationale.C: the river is not a character

questions.explanation: A third-person narrator can show every character's actions.
questions.rule: RL.5.6 — point of view shapes what is told.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that shows the goats understood their mistake.
questions.rubric: Accept: "We could easily have done that," said the white goat in a quiet voice. OR "but we were far too busy being right." OR the final sentence about stepping aside. Must be a quoted sentence from the text that shows the lesson learned.
questions.explanation: The white goat's quiet words show he sees what they should have done.

passages.title: The Ant Who Saved the Summer
passages.text: Inside a walled garden on the eastern edge of Baku, an ant named Nara laboured steadily through the hottest weeks of summer. Every morning she carried seeds across the dusty path to the family nest beneath the ancient fig tree. Her cousin Tofiq preferred to recline in the shade of a broad leaf, where he could observe her efforts without lifting a single leg. "The sun is shining and the garden is overflowing with food," he remarked lazily. "Why do you exhaust yourself when you could simply relax?" Nara brushed the dust from her feelers and glanced at the brilliant sky. "The sun will not shine forever," she answered, and returned immediately to her carrying. Tofiq ignored every word of the warning. He devoted his days to chasing drops of honey and entertaining the patient beetles with jokes. Then summer ended, as summers always do, and the weather changed completely. The rains arrived first, and after the rains came the bitter cold. The garden faded to brown, the flowers closed, and every seed along the path disappeared. Tofiq searched through the soaking leaves for hours and discovered nothing whatsoever. His stomach ached and his legs trembled with hunger and exhaustion. Finally he crawled to the fig tree and knocked feebly on the door of Nara's nest. Nara opened it, and behind her Tofiq glimpsed chambers that were warm and generously stocked with food. He stared at the floor because he could not bring himself to meet her eyes. "You were right," he admitted quietly. "I should have helped you instead of laughing." Nara remained silent for a moment, remembering how exhausted she had been and how loudly he had laughed. Then she stepped aside and held the door open. "Come in," she said, "but when spring arrives, you will carry seeds as well." Tofiq nodded gratefully and stumbled inside. Throughout that winter he learned to count the seeds and mend the walls of the nest. When spring finally returned, he was the first ant through the door, and he carried two seeds at a time.

questions.stem: What did Nara do all summer?
options: She told jokes to the beetles.
She carried seeds to her nest.
She slept under the fig tree.
questions.explanation: The text says she carried seeds to the nest every morning.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the theme?
options: Prepare now for harder times later.
questions.explanation: Nara's planning keeps her safe; Tofiq learns to prepare.

questions.stem: "He learned to count the seeds and mend the walls of the nest." What does "mend" mean?

distractor_rationale.D: counting is a separate action in the sentence

questions.explanation: Mending walls means fixing them.
questions.rule: L.5.4a — context clue: the walls need fixing in winter.

questions.stem: How does Tofiq change from the beginning to the end of the story?
options: He goes from working hard to being lazy.
He goes from laughing at work to doing it first.
He moves to a different garden.
questions.explanation: At the end he is the first ant through the door and carries two seeds.
questions.rule: RL.5.3 — compare a character across the story.

questions.stem: "The sun will not shine forever." What does Nara really mean?
options: Good times end, so prepare for hard times.
She wants Tofiq to move out of the shade.
questions.explanation: It is a figurative way of saying summer will end.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that shows Nara forgave Tofiq.
questions.rubric: Accept: Then she stepped aside and held the door open. OR "Come in," she said, "but when spring arrives, you will carry seeds as well." Must quote a sentence showing she lets him in.
questions.explanation: Stepping aside and saying 'Come in' shows forgiveness.

passages.title: The Crow and the Water Jar
passages.text: A thirsty crow flew slowly over a parched field on a scorching afternoon in late August. She had not discovered a single drop of water since the early morning. Her throat felt rough, her wings felt heavy, and the ground beneath her shimmered with heat. Eventually she noticed a tall clay jar standing beside an abandoned well. She landed on its rim and peered inside with one bright, curious eye. There was water at the bottom, but only a little, and the jar was tall and extremely narrow. When she pushed her beak inside, it stopped far above the surface of the water. She attempted to tip the jar over with her feet, but it was much too heavy to move. She attempted to crack it with her beak, but the clay was as hard as stone. The crow settled on the rim and considered the problem for a long time. Scattered around the well lay dozens of small grey pebbles. She picked one up, carried it to the jar, and dropped it inside. It fell with a tiny splash, and the water rose by the smallest amount. She dropped another pebble, and then another, watching carefully every time. With every pebble the water climbed a little higher inside the jar. It was slow, exhausting work, and her wings ached from the effort. Nevertheless she did not stop. After forty pebbles the water finally reached the top of the jar. The crow drank until her throat was cool and her head felt clear again. Then she flew to the shade of a fig tree to recover. A young sparrow who had been watching hopped closer along the branch. "How did you know that idea would succeed?" he asked in wonder. The crow closed her eyes against the afternoon sun. "I did not know," she replied. "I only knew that pushing and breaking had failed. So I tried something small, many times over."

questions.stem: Why couldn't the crow reach the water at first?
options: The jar was tall and narrow, and the water was low.
The sparrow was in the way.
questions.explanation: Her beak stopped far above the water because the jar was tall and narrow.

questions.stem: What is the message of the story?
options: Strong birds get what they want.
Small steps, repeated with patience, can solve a hard problem.
questions.explanation: Forty small pebbles did what pushing and breaking could not.

questions.stem: "She landed on its rim and peered inside with one bright, curious eye." What is the "rim"?
options: the top edge of the jar
questions.explanation: The rim is the edge at the top.

questions.stem: How is the story organised?
options: A problem, several failed attempts, then a solution.
A list of facts about crows.
A conversation between two birds only.
Events told backwards from the end.

distractor_rationale.C: the talk comes at the end

questions.explanation: Problem → tipping fails → cracking fails → pebbles work.
questions.rule: RL.5.5 — how parts of a story fit together.

questions.stem: Whose point of view does the narrator mostly follow?

distractor_rationale.A: the sparrow appears only at the end

questions.explanation: We follow the crow's feelings and thoughts.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that explains the crow's strategy in her own words.
questions.rubric: Accept: "So I tried something small, many times over." (with or without the previous sentence). Must be a quotation, not a paraphrase.
questions.explanation: That sentence names the strategy: small, repeated tries.

passages.title: The Shepherd's Whistle
passages.text: In a village beneath the Caucasus mountains lived a boy named Ilgar, whose family entrusted him with their sheep. Every morning he guided the flock up the green slope above the houses and remained with them until evening. It was quiet, solitary work, and Ilgar was frequently bored. One afternoon, for no reason except boredom, he blew the alarm whistle that hung around his neck. Three sharp notes carried one message to everybody in the valley: a wolf was threatening the flock. The villagers abandoned their tools and hurried up the hill as quickly as they could. They discovered Ilgar sitting on a boulder, laughing until tears ran down his cheeks. "There is no wolf," he announced. "I only wanted to see how fast you could run." The villagers were furious, but they said little and returned to their work. A week later, Ilgar blew the whistle again, and again there was no wolf anywhere. Fewer people climbed the hill that time, and they climbed considerably more slowly. "Do not play games with that whistle," warned old Sona, leaning on her walking stick. "One day you will genuinely need it, and nobody will come." Ilgar merely shrugged and turned back to the sheep. Then, on a grey morning in autumn, a real wolf slipped silently out of the forest. It was thin and hungry, and it moved without disturbing a single leaf. Ilgar blew the whistle with all the breath in his body, three notes and then three more. Down in the village, people glanced up at the hill for a moment. "It is only the boy again," they said, and carried on with their work. Only old Sona collected her stick and began the long, painful climb. By the time she reached the slope, the wolf had seized a lamb and vanished. Ilgar stood trembling beside the frightened flock, unable to speak. Sona rested a hand on his shoulder and waited until he could look at her. "A whistle is only as good as the boy who blows it," she said. Ilgar never blew a false alarm again. It took a long time before the villagers ran when they heard his whistle, but eventually, they did.

questions.stem: What did three sharp notes on the whistle mean?
options: A wolf is threatening the flock.
questions.explanation: The text says three sharp notes meant a wolf was threatening the flock.

questions.stem: What lesson does Ilgar learn?
options: Sheep are more important than people.
If you lie for fun, people stop believing you when it matters.

distractor_rationale.C: Sona is the one who comes

questions.explanation: His false alarms cost him the villagers' trust.

questions.stem: "Ilgar never blew a false alarm again." What is a "false alarm"?
options: a warning about a danger that is not real
questions.explanation: He blew the whistle when there was no wolf.

questions.stem: "A whistle is only as good as the boy who blows it." What does Sona mean?
options: The whistle needs a new string.
A warning only works if people trust the person giving it.
questions.explanation: The whistle's power depends on Ilgar's honesty.

questions.stem: How is Sona different from the other villagers?
options: She is the only one who still comes when the whistle sounds.

distractor_rationale.B: she is old and has a stick

questions.explanation: Only Sona climbs the hill the third time.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that shows the villagers no longer believed Ilgar.
questions.rubric: Accept: "It is only the boy again," they said, and carried on with their work. Must quote that sentence (or its first part).
questions.explanation: They dismiss the alarm as the boy's game.

passages.title: The Lantern Race
passages.text: Every spring, the children of Qala organised a lantern race along the wide, windswept shore. Each runner carried a paper lantern with a small candle flickering inside it. The winner was the first to reach the ancient stone tower with the flame still burning. Sabina had trained for the race every evening for six weeks without missing a day. She could run the entire length of the beach without pausing for breath. Her friend Kamran was slower, but he was clever with his hands and patient with details. He had constructed his lantern with a tiny window that protected the candle from the wind. The race began just as the sun touched the horizon. Sabina surged ahead immediately, and the sand flew up behind her feet. Halfway to the tower, a sudden gust of wind swept in from the sea. Her candle flickered twice and went out, leaving her lantern completely dark. She stopped and stared at it, unable to believe what had happened. The other runners passed her one by one, their lanterns glowing like miniature moons. Then Kamran arrived, breathing hard, with his own lantern still shining steadily. He looked at her dark lantern, then at the distant tower, and then at her face. Without saying a word, he opened his little window and touched his flame to her wick. Her candle caught and steadied. "Go on," he said. "You are faster than me." Sabina did not move. "We go together," she said. They walked the final stretch side by side, shielding each other's flames with their hands. They reached the tower last of all the competitors. The judge frowned at them for a moment, and then she laughed aloud. "Two lanterns, both still burning," she said. "I have never seen that in twenty years." She presented them with one small prize to share between them. Sabina still keeps it on the shelf above her bed. She says it is the only race she ever lost and won at the same time.

questions.stem: How did a runner win the lantern race?
options: By running the fastest, even with a dark lantern.
By reaching the tower first with the flame still burning.

distractor_rationale.A: the flame had to be lit

questions.explanation: The text states the rule in the third sentence.

questions.stem: How are Sabina and Kamran different?
options: Sabina is fast; Kamran is clever with his hands.
Sabina is clever; Kamran is fast.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph contrasts their strengths.

questions.stem: What is the theme of the story?
options: Winning is the only thing that matters.
Helping a friend can matter more than winning.
questions.explanation: Kamran gives up his chance to win to relight Sabina's lantern.

questions.stem: "They walked the final stretch side by side, shielding each other's flames." What does "shielding" mean?

distractor_rationale.D: carrying is not the same as protecting

questions.explanation: They protect the flames from the wind.
questions.rule: L.5.4a — context clue: with their hands, against the wind.

questions.stem: "The only race she ever lost and won at the same time." What does this mean?
options: She came last but gained something better than a prize.
She won a bigger prize later.

distractor_rationale.A: the judge laughed and gave a prize

questions.explanation: She lost the race but won a friendship and a shared prize.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that shows Kamran chose to help instead of racing on.
questions.rubric: Accept: Without saying a word, he opened his little window and touched his flame to her wick. Must be that sentence.
questions.explanation: That sentence shows his choice.

passages.title: The Girl Who Counted Stars
passages.text: Leyla had decided to count every single star in the sky above her house. Her older brother informed her that this was completely impossible. "There are millions of them," he explained. "You will fall asleep before you reach a hundred." Leyla did not bother to argue with him. She carried a notebook and a pencil up to the flat roof and began. On the first night she counted forty stars and then lost her place among them. On the second night she reached sixty before a thick cloud covered the entire sky. Her brother laughed at her from the window below, and Leyla pretended not to hear. On the third night, she tried something completely different. She held up her fingers and framed a small square of sky between them. Then she counted only the stars inside that square, which turned out to be twelve. She moved the square to the left and counted again, and this time there were nine. She moved it once more and counted eleven. Before long she had filled an entire page with small, careful numbers. In the morning she showed the page to her grandfather over breakfast. He put on his glasses and studied it for a long time without speaking. "You have not counted every star," he observed at last. "No," agreed Leyla, "but I know roughly how many there are. I counted the squares, then multiplied." Her grandfather smiled and set down his tea. "That," he said, "is exactly what astronomers do." That afternoon he took her to the library and found a book with a photograph of the night sky. It showed more stars than Leyla had ever imagined, thousands upon thousands of them. She was not discouraged for a moment. She turned to a clean page in her notebook and drew a new square. Her brother watched from the doorway with his arms folded. After a while he came in, sat down beside her, and asked how the squares worked.

questions.stem: What went wrong on the second night?
options: A thick cloud covered the sky.
questions.explanation: The text says a thick cloud covered the entire sky.

questions.stem: What is the main message of the story?
options: Some problems cannot be solved, so give up.
A clever method can make an impossible task possible.
questions.explanation: Leyla's square method turns an impossible count into an estimate.

questions.stem: "She was not discouraged for a moment." What does "discouraged" mean?
questions.explanation: Seeing so many stars could have made her give up, but it did not.

questions.stem: How does Leyla's brother change during the story?
options: He starts helpful and becomes unkind.
He starts by laughing and ends by wanting to learn.
He moves to the roof permanently.
questions.explanation: At the end he sits beside her and asks how the squares work.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe three nights one after another?
options: To show that each attempt teaches Leyla something and leads to her new method.
To show the brother was right.
questions.explanation: Each failed night leads to the idea of the square.
questions.rule: RL.5.5 — how scenes build on one another.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence in which Leyla explains her method.
questions.rubric: Accept: "I counted the squares, then multiplied." (with or without the sentence before it). Must be a quotation.
questions.explanation: That sentence names the method.

passages.title: The Baker's Apprentice
passages.text: Rasim had been employed at the bakery on Nizami Street for exactly one week, and so far he had learned only how to sweep the floor and stack the heavy trays. Today, for the very first time, Master Farid was allowing him to prepare the bread himself. "Two cups of water," said Farid, counting slowly on his fingers. "Then the yeast, then the flour, and then you wait patiently." Rasim nodded eagerly, but he was so excited that he poured the flour into the bowl first. Then he added the water, and then he could not find the yeast anywhere. By the time he discovered it behind the sugar, the dough had become a hard grey lump. He kneaded and kneaded until his arms were exhausted, but nothing improved. He placed the lump in the oven anyway and hoped for a miracle. An hour later he pulled out a loaf as flat and heavy as a brick. Rasim's face burned with embarrassment. He wanted to bury the loaf at the bottom of the bin before Farid could notice it. Instead, he carried it slowly to the counter and set it down. "I did the steps in the wrong order," he confessed. Farid picked up the loaf and knocked on it with his knuckles. It sounded exactly like a stone, and Rasim waited miserably for the shouting to begin. Then Farid did something his apprentice had not expected at all. He laughed, cut a thin slice, and ate it thoughtfully. "Salty," he said, chewing and nodding. "But you told me the truth, and you understand precisely what went wrong. That is worth more to me than one good loaf." He handed Rasim a clean bowl and a fresh packet of yeast. "Again," he said. "Water first this time." The second loaf rose golden and light, and the customers bought every slice before noon. Rasim kept the flat loaf on the shelf above the oven for an entire year. Whenever he felt too sure of himself, he looked up at it and remembered.

questions.stem: What was the correct order for making the bread?
questions.explanation: Farid says: two cups of water, then the yeast, then the flour.

questions.stem: What is the theme of the story?
options: Honesty about a mistake is worth more than hiding it.
Bread must be baked for one hour.
Apprentices should not touch the oven.
questions.explanation: Farid values Rasim's truthfulness more than the loaf.

questions.stem: "Rasim nodded eagerly, but he was so excited that he poured the flour into the bowl first." What does "eagerly" mean?
questions.explanation: His eagerness made him rush.

questions.stem: "A loaf as flat and heavy as a brick." What kind of language is this, and why is it used?
options: A simile, to show how badly the bread turned out.
A metaphor, to show the bread was made of clay.
A fact, because bread is a building material.

distractor_rationale.B: 'as … as' is a simile, and the bread is not clay

questions.explanation: 'As flat and heavy as a brick' compares using 'as'.

questions.stem: From whose point of view do we experience the story?

distractor_rationale.A: we do not know Farid's thoughts
distractor_rationale.C: customers appear only at the end

questions.explanation: We know Rasim's feelings, such as his burning face.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that shows Rasim decided not to hide his mistake.
questions.rubric: Accept: Instead, he carried it slowly to the counter and set it down. OR "I did the steps in the wrong order," he confessed. Must quote one of these.
questions.explanation: Carrying the loaf to the counter is the decision.

passages.title: The Key in the Fountain
passages.text: The fountain in the old town square had been dry for as long as anyone could remember. Nigar enjoyed sitting on its stone edge in the afternoons with a library book. One warm Saturday she accidentally dropped her pencil into the empty basin. When she climbed in to retrieve it, she noticed something glinting between two loose stones. It was a small iron key, green with age, and on its handle was a tiny carving of a fish. Nigar carried the key across the square to her uncle, who repaired clocks in the shop opposite the fountain. He turned it over slowly in his careful, experienced hands. "A fish," he murmured. "There was a fish shop on this square before the war. My grandmother used to describe it to me." "Where exactly was it?" asked Nigar, already halfway to the door. He pointed through the window at a bakery with a faded blue door. Nigar went inside and politely asked the baker whether she could examine his cellar. The baker was astonished by the question, but he liked Nigar, and he handed her a lamp. The cellar was cold and smelled of flour and damp stone. In the far wall stood a low wooden door with an iron lock. Nigar's heart thumped as she fitted the key into the keyhole. It turned with a rusty squeak, and the door swung slowly open. Behind it was a tiny room lined with wooden shelves from floor to ceiling. On the shelves stood rows of glass jars, each with a label written in faded ink. Inside the jars were shells, dried seaweed, and the delicate bones of tiny fish. There was also a notebook, bound in cracked brown leather. The first page said: "Collected from the Caspian shore, 1938." Nigar carried the notebook up into the light of the shop. The baker read it over her shoulder and shook his head in amazement. "A hidden museum," he whispered, "underneath my bread all these years." Today the jars stand in a glass case in the town library, beside a card that records who discovered them.

questions.stem: Where did Nigar find the key?
options: Between two loose stones in the dry fountain

distractor_rationale.A: that is where the door was

questions.explanation: She saw it glinting between two loose stones in the basin.

questions.stem: What clue leads Nigar from the fountain to the bakery?
options: The carving of a fish on the key

distractor_rationale.A: the pencil only leads her into the fountain
distractor_rationale.C: the door is where the shop was, not the clue

questions.explanation: The fish carving reminds her uncle of the old fish shop.

questions.stem: "She noticed something glinting between two loose stones." What does "glinting" mean?
questions.explanation: The key catches the light.

questions.stem: Which idea does the story most support?
options: Curiosity and asking questions can uncover hidden things.
questions.explanation: Nigar's questions lead to the hidden museum.

questions.stem: The last sentence jumps to 'today'. What does this change of time tell the reader?
options: That the story was a dream.
That Nigar's discovery mattered and was shared with everyone.
That the fountain has water again.

distractor_rationale.C: they are in a glass case

questions.explanation: The narrator steps forward in time to show the result.

questions.stem: Quote the sentence that tells when the collection was made.
questions.rubric: Accept: The first page said: "Collected from the Caspian shore, 1938." (or just the quoted label). Must include 1938.
questions.explanation: The notebook's first page gives the date.
